acts.title: Creation
acts.summary:
The Bible does not open with rules or with religion. It opens with a maker. In the beginning God speaks, and where there was nothing there is light, sky, sea, land, and every living thing. Six times he stops to look at what he has made and calls it good. This is not a cold machine winding itself up. It is a home being built by someone who delights in it.

Then God makes one creature unlike the rest. He makes human beings in his own image, male and female, and he gives them a place and a calling. They are to fill the earth, to care for it, and to rule it under him as gardeners rule a garden. Work is not a curse here. It is a gift. Adam names the animals. The woman is given as a partner, bone of his bone. The two become one flesh and feel no shame.

At the center of the garden stands the deepest thing of all. God walks with the people he has made. There is no temple yet because the whole world is the temple, and God is present in it. Everything is exactly as it should be. The first note the Bible sounds is not guilt. It is gladness.
acts.turning: God makes human beings in his own image and gives them his world to keep and rule under him.
acts.pointsForward: The good world we were made for is the world the whole story will work to win back, and the true image-bearer who finally rules it well will be Christ.

acts.title: The Fall
acts.summary:
There was one tree the people were told to leave alone, one place to trust God instead of grasping for themselves. A voice came into the garden and turned the gift into a suspicion. Did God really say. Maybe he is holding out on you. The man and the woman reached for the fruit, and in that reaching something broke that has never since been whole. They hid from the God who walked with them. They blamed each other. They were sent out of the garden, and an angel with a flaming sword stood at the gate.

The damage spreads fast. The first children grow up and one murders the other. Violence fills the earth until God sends a flood and starts again with one family in an ark, yet sin climbs out of the boat with them. At last the people gather on a plain and build a tower to make a name for themselves, reaching up to heaven on their own terms. God scatters them and confuses their speech, and the human family is broken into nations that cannot understand each other.

But even in the ruin of the garden, God makes a promise. He tells the serpent that a child of the woman will one day crush its head, though the serpent will strike his heel. It is the first thread of hope in a dark chapter. Someone is coming who will undo what was done here.
acts.turning: Trust is traded for grasping, sin floods the world, and yet God promises a deliverer born of the woman.
acts.pointsForward: The promise of a child who will crush the serpent sets the whole story leaning toward the one who will be wounded to win, which is Christ on the cross.

acts.title: Abraham and the Promise
acts.summary:
Into a world scattered and far from God, the maker speaks to one old man. Leave your country, God says to Abraham, and go to a land I will show you. I will make you into a great nation, and through you all the families of the earth will be blessed. Abraham has no children and his wife cannot have them, yet he goes. He believes God, and God counts that belief as righteousness. The plan to heal the whole world begins with one family and one promise.

The promise is tested again and again. Decades pass before the son Isaac is born. Then God asks Abraham to give that very son back, and at the last moment provides a ram in his place. The story narrows to Isaac, then to Jacob, a deceiver whom God refuses to abandon and even renames Israel. Jacob has twelve sons, and the family becomes a clan.

It nearly dies in jealousy. The brothers sell young Joseph into slavery in Egypt, but God is at work in the dark. Joseph rises to power and, when famine strikes, saves the very brothers who betrayed him. What you meant for evil, he tells them, God meant for good. The family of promise survives, sheltered in Egypt, waiting for what God will do next.
acts.turning: God chooses one childless man and binds himself by promise to bless every family of the earth through his offspring.
acts.pointsForward: The promise that all nations would be blessed through Abraham's family finds its yes in Jesus, the offspring through whom the blessing finally reaches the world.

acts.title: Exodus and Sinai
acts.summary:
Years go by and the family becomes a people, and the people become slaves. A new king of Egypt fears them and grinds them under hard labor and orders their sons drowned. They cry out, and God hears. He remembers his promise to Abraham. He raises up Moses, a fugitive shepherd, and speaks to him from a bush that burns but is not consumed. I have seen the misery of my people, God says. I am sending you to bring them out.

What follows is the great rescue. Plague after plague falls on Egypt until the last terrible night, when death passes over every house marked by the blood of a lamb. Pharaoh lets them go. The sea opens before them and closes behind them, and a nation of former slaves walks free onto dry ground. They sing on the far shore. This is the moment Israel will tell its children about forever.

God brings them to a mountain called Sinai and gives them his law, beginning with ten words carved in stone. He is not only rescuing them from something. He is binding them to himself. You will be my people, he says, and I will be your God. Then comes the most astonishing instruction of all. Build me a tent, a tabernacle, so that I may dwell among you. The God of the burning bush comes down to live in the middle of the camp.
acts.turning: God hears the cry of slaves, rescues them through the blood of a lamb and the open sea, and comes down to dwell among them.
acts.pointsForward: The Passover lamb, the rescue from bondage, and God coming to live with his people all point ahead to Jesus, the Lamb of God who frees us and the Word made flesh who dwells among us.

acts.title: The Land and the Judges
acts.summary:
After Moses dies, Joshua leads the people across the Jordan into the land God had promised to Abraham long before. City by city they enter the inheritance. For a while it looks like the story has arrived at its rest. They have a land, they have the law, and they have the presence of God among them. The long ache of slavery is behind them.

Then comes a pattern that breaks the heart by repetition. The people forget. They turn to the gods of the nations around them. Trouble falls on them, they cry out, and God in mercy raises up a judge to rescue them. There is peace for a time. Then they forget again. Around and around it goes, each turn a little lower than the last, until the closing line of the book of Judges admits the whole problem. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes.

Yet inside the chaos there is a quiet, shining story. A foreign widow named Ruth clings to the God of Israel and to her bitter mother in law, and gleans in the fields of a kind man named Boaz, who takes her as his wife. From this unlikely and tender union comes a son, and from that line, in time, will come a king named David. God is writing a thread of grace through the mess.
acts.turning: Israel enters the promised land but falls into a cycle of forgetting God, being rescued, and forgetting again.
acts.pointsForward: The endless need for a rescuer and the quiet line of Ruth toward David both reach for a king who will not fail and a rest the land could never finally give, found at last in Christ.

acts.title: The Kingdom
acts.summary:
The people demand a king like the other nations have. Their first king, Saul, looks the part and then crumbles. So God chooses a shepherd boy, the youngest son of Jesse, a man after his own heart. David kills the giant Goliath with a sling, waits years for a throne he will not seize by force, and at last unites the people. He is a flawed man, an adulterer and far worse, yet he loves God truly and repents deeply, and God makes him a staggering promise. One of your sons will sit on a throne that will last forever.

David's son Solomon builds the temple, a permanent home for the presence of God, and for a golden moment the kingdom is wide and rich and at peace. Kings and queens come from far away to hear Solomon's wisdom. It feels like the high tide of the whole story, the garden almost regained.

But Solomon's heart drifts to other gods, and after him the kingdom tears in two. Israel in the north and Judah in the south stumble through a long line of mostly faithless kings. A few are good. Most lead the people deeper into idolatry and injustice. The temple stands, but the glory is fading, and the prophets begin to warn that the borrowed time is running out.
acts.turning: God promises David a son whose throne will last forever, even as the kingdom rises in glory and then slides toward ruin.
acts.pointsForward: The promise of an everlasting throne to David's house waits for a greater son, Jesus, the king whose reign truly never ends.

acts.title: The Prophets and Exile
acts.summary:
For generations God sends prophets to plead with his people. They are not fortune tellers. They are covenant lawyers and brokenhearted poets, men like Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Amos, and Hosea, who name the sin no one wants named. You have abandoned the God who loves you, they say. You crush the poor, you worship idols, you trust in armies and alliances instead of in the Lord. Turn back before it is too late.

The people will not turn, and the warning comes true. The northern kingdom falls to Assyria. Then Babylon comes for the south, breaks down the walls of Jerusalem, and burns the temple to the ground. The presence of God seems to leave. The people are dragged into exile far from home. The book of Lamentations sits in the ashes and weeps. How lonely sits the city that once was full of people.

And yet, exactly here, in the worst chapter, the prophets sing their highest songs. God is not finished. He promises a new covenant, one written not on stone but on the heart. He promises to gather his scattered people, to pour out his Spirit, to raise up a shepherd king from David's line, and to make a servant who will bear the sins of many and be pierced for our transgressions. Out of the darkness, the promise burns brighter than ever.
acts.turning: The people refuse the prophets, the temple falls and exile comes, and yet God promises a new covenant and a coming king.
acts.pointsForward: The promised new covenant written on the heart, the suffering servant pierced for us, and the shepherd king all describe Jesus before he is born.

acts.title: The Return and the Silence
acts.range: Ezra, Nehemiah, Esther, Malachi, and the Years Between
acts.summary:
After seventy years, a door opens. The empire that conquered Babylon lets the exiles go home. A remnant returns to a ruined Jerusalem. Under leaders like Ezra and Nehemiah they rebuild the temple, though the old men who remember the first one weep because this one is so much smaller. They raise the city walls under threat and reopen the book of the law and weep again to hear it read. Far away in Persia, a young woman named Esther risks her life and saves her people from being wiped out, and God works to protect the line of promise even when his name is never spoken aloud.

It is a real homecoming, but it is not the homecoming the prophets had described. There is no king on David's throne. The glory has not filled the temple as before. The grand promises of a new covenant and a poured out Spirit hang in the air, unfulfilled. The last prophet, Malachi, closes the Old Testament looking forward, promising a messenger who will prepare the way and a sun of righteousness that will rise with healing.

Then, for about four hundred years, heaven goes quiet. No prophet speaks. Empires rise and fall over the little land. The people wait, and read the old scrolls, and hope, and ask the only question left to ask. When will God keep his word and come.
acts.turning: A remnant comes home and rebuilds, but the great promises remain unkept, and four centuries of silence follow.
acts.pointsForward: The whole Old Testament ends leaning forward into the dark, waiting for the messenger and the rising sun, and the next sound it hears will be the announcement of Jesus.

acts.title: Christ, the Center
acts.summary:
The silence breaks with a baby. In a backwater town, in a feeding trough, the maker of the world is born as a child. Angels tell shepherds the news. Wise men follow a star. The promised messenger, John, grows up and points to him and says, look, the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world. Everything the story has been reaching for since the garden is standing there in a man named Jesus.

He goes about doing things only God can do and saying things only God would dare to say. He heals the sick, opens blind eyes, calms storms, and welcomes the very people the religious despise. He forgives sins. He teaches that the kingdom of God has come near, and he lives the perfect human life that Adam and Israel never could. He is the true image-bearer, the true son, the king from David's line, God himself come to dwell among us at last.

And then he does what he came to do. He is betrayed, arrested, and nailed to a cross, and there the serpent strikes his heel. He takes the judgment we earned. The temple curtain tears from top to bottom. He is buried. But on the third day the tomb is empty, and he is alive, and death itself is broken. The heel was struck, but the serpent's head was crushed. The whole story turns on this hinge.
acts.turning: God himself comes as Jesus, lives the life we could not, dies the death we deserved, and rises to break death forever.
acts.pointsForward: Every promise from the garden to the prophets meets its yes in the risen Christ, and now the good news of what he has done begins to go out to the world.

acts.title: The Church and the Spirit
acts.summary:
Before he returns to his Father, the risen Jesus gives his followers a charge. Go and make disciples of all nations. Then, just as the prophets had promised, God pours out his Spirit. On the day of Pentecost the Spirit falls on a frightened band of disciples, and they spill into the streets speaking of Jesus, and three thousand people believe in a single day. The new people of God is born, not bound to one nation but open to every nation, exactly as God told Abraham it would be.

The good news runs outward like a fire. A man named Saul, who hunted Christians, meets the risen Jesus on a road and becomes Paul, the great messenger to the nations. The gospel crosses from Jews to Gentiles, from Jerusalem to the heart of the empire. Ordinary people in ordinary cities are knit into one family across every old division. The scattering of Babel begins to be healed in reverse.

The letters that fill out this act are the apostles teaching these young churches how to live as the people of the new covenant. They explain what the cross accomplished, they correct and encourage, they call believers to love one another and to hold fast under pressure. And through all of it runs a steady forward lean, a waiting and a watching, because the king who came once has promised to come again.
acts.turning: The Spirit is poured out, the church is born, and the good news of Jesus crosses every nation just as God promised Abraham.
acts.pointsForward: The new people of God live between the king's first coming and his last, carrying the good news outward while they wait for him to return and make all things new.

acts.title: The New Creation
acts.summary:
The Bible ends where it began, in a garden, only now it is also a city, and it is better than the first. The book of Revelation pulls back the curtain on where the whole story is heading. The king who came as a lamb returns as a conquering king. Evil is finally judged. The serpent who whispered in the garden, the power behind every empire and every cruelty, is thrown down for good. Every tear of every exile is accounted for.

Then comes the sight the prophets longed for and could barely describe. A new heaven and a new earth. The home of God is now among his people. He will live with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them. He will wipe every tear from their eyes, and there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain, for the old order of things has passed away.

There is no temple in the city, because the Lord himself is its temple, and no sun, because the glory of God is its light. The river of life runs through it, and the tree of life grows there, its leaves for the healing of the nations. The gates never close. The curse is gone. What was lost in the third chapter of the story is more than restored in the last. And the final word of the whole book is a prayer of longing and a promise kept. Come, Lord Jesus.
acts.turning: The king returns, evil is judged forever, and God comes down to dwell with his people in a renewed world without tears.
acts.pointsForward: The story that began with God walking in a garden ends with God dwelling among his people forever, and every thread from Genesis onward is gathered up and kept in Christ.
